sheets.summary: Based on lectures by Rabbi Dr. Ira Bedzow and tomes by Yuval Noah Harari, we are presently challenged to define what is human for the purposes of Jewish law and living in a civilized, ethical society.  How Torah defines a human is a starting point only.

Anthropomorphism of God

Sefaria worksheet raising the question over anthropomorphism of God in Judaism. How has the image of God changed over time? 

Created by Jon Laxdal and Abdur Khan
sheets.attribution: Source Sheet by Jon Laxdal and Abdur Khan

sheets.title: The Different Opinions on Btzelem Elokim
sheets.summary:
At humanity's point of origin, the Torah tells us that Hashem made us "btzelem Elokim," in His image. The significance of this is not lost on us, but the details behind such significance sometimes are. 

Which part of us was made btzelem Elokim? What are the possibilities? How do we practically understand that? 

This source sheet presents four different opinions or "camps" on btzelem Elokim's meaning, and while it is not all-inclusive, the hope is that it close to that.  

(Main credit is to Rav Dovid'll Weinberg for these sources)

description.en: Many biblical and rabbinic sources describe God using the language of physicality, but influential rabbinic texts emphasize that denial of God's physicality is a [key principle of Jewish faith](https://www.sefaria.org/Rambam_on_Mishnah_Sanhedrin.10.1.18?lang=en). Philosophers, scholars, kabbalists, and commentators have all attempted to explain how a transcendent God can be described in human terms. A few have maintained that God does or could indeed possess a physical form, some have interpreted physical language in traditional sources metaphorically, and some have reinterpreted it in light of kabbalistic concepts.
